Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short evidence-based questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during these first weeks of motherhood. Nothing you share leaves this room, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you today. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; each one usually takes only a moment to answer. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Hi, Sarah. I… I can still laugh, I guess, but it feels like I have to remind myself to. I watched a sitcom the other night and chuckled a couple of times, yet it didn’t feel as easy or natural as it used to—like the joy is muted.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh, but it’s not the same. Like, I’ll smile at something silly the baby does, or a joke my husband makes, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m going through the motions. It doesn’t come as naturally as it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like my mom coming over or taking the baby for a walk if the weather’s nice—but the excitement is kind of muted. Before the baby I’d feel this bubbly “can’t-wait” feeling, and now it’s more like “I guess that’ll be nice.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was fussy for an hour and I kept thinking maybe I’d eaten something that upset her stomach, or that I wasn’t soothing her right. Rationally I know babies just cry sometimes, but I still had this little voice saying, “You must’ve done something wrong.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly wonder if she’s breathing okay, or I’ll check the monitor three times even though she’s clearly asleep. It’s not constant, and I can usually talk myself down, but it pops up out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—just that fluttery, on-edge feeling every so often. It’s like my heart speeds up for a minute when I imagine something random happening to her, but it passes pretty quickly. I haven’t had any full-blown panic spells.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yes. It’s not every moment, but there are times—especially when she won’t settle at 3 a.m.—where I feel like I’m juggling more plates than I can handle. I usually get through it, but it leaves me a bit frazzled.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, not really. I mean, I’m tired, and sometimes it takes me a little while to fall asleep because my mind races a bit, but once I’m out I stay asleep—unless she wakes me. I haven’t felt so upset that it kept me up.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel kind of sad some of the day, maybe every other day. It’s not all the time, but little things—like seeing other moms looking cheerful on social media or when the baby won’t nap—make me tear up or feel blue for a while.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… probably once or twice this week. I got overwhelmed when she wouldn’t latch, and another time I just sat in the rocker and teared up because I felt like I wasn’t doing enough. It wasn’t all-day sobbing—just quiet crying that lasted a few minutes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself at all.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Screening note – 2 wk postpartum  
Patient describes:  
- Dysthymic mood most days, intermittent tearfulness (Q8-9)  
- Marked reduction in pleasure/enthusiasm for previously enjoyable activities (Q1-2)  
- Self-blame and guilt when infant fussy (Q3)  
- Recurrent, unfocused worries about infant safety; mild physiologic arousal but no panic attacks (Q4-5)  
- Episodic feeling “frazzled/overloaded,” especially during night-time infant care (Q6)  
- Occasional sleep-onset latency related to racing thoughts; no sustained insomnia (Q7)  
- Denies any self-harm ideation (Q10)  

Pattern consistent with subsyndromal/early postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; does not currently meet threshold for major depression but indicates distress and impaired coping. Recommend routine Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score, psycho-education, support linkage, and re-screen in 1-2 wks to monitor trajectory.
